# Turn Signal Clicks Randomly

A single, unprovoked click from a turn signal relay can be disconcerting, especially when it happens in cool, humid weather or coincides with pressing the brake pedal. In the case of a 1994 Jeep Grand Cherokee, this symptom emerged after replacing an intermittent relay that previously caused signals to fail completely. While the new unit resolved the "no blink" issues, the behavior describedâa long initial delay followed by rapid clicking upon braking and activating the rear defrosterâsuggests a specific electrical interaction rather than a simple mechanical fault.

The most prominent clue is the environmental dependency: symptoms worsen in cold, humid conditions and improve as the vehicle warms up. This strongly points to moisture condensation or corrosion acting on internal contacts. When humidity is high, thin films of water can form on metal surfaces within the relay housing or at the connector pins. These conductive paths create unintended leakage currents. The long initial blink (a full second before settling into rhythm) indicates that the relay coil or switch has a slight "stiction" issue, where moisture temporarily increases contact resistance until the first high-current pulse burns off the water film or heats the component enough to dry it out.

The correlation with the brake pedal and rear defroster is particularly telling. Pressing the brake pedal completes the ground path for the brake lights. If the turn signal switch shares a common ground strap or grounding point with the brake lights, that extra load can shift the voltage at the relay's ground pin. In a system with corroded connections, this slight voltage drop might be enough to trigger false triggering of the relay coil, causing the single click without activating the bulbs. Similarly, the rear defroster adds significant load to the 12V electrical system. If the vehicle has poor grounding elsewhere, this surge in current demand can cause a momentary dip in battery voltage or a shift in ground potential, exacerbating the erratic behavior of an already marginal relay connection.

From a developer's perspective, this is analogous to debugging a hardware interface where a floating input pin occasionally triggers a state change due to noise on the power rail. You cannot fix the logic in software if the physical layer is unstable. The "jamming" sound describedârapid clicksâis likely the relay chatter cycle: the coil energizes briefly, the contacts close and arc, causing a voltage drop that drops the coil current below the threshold needed to stay latched, then it re-energizes. This creates an oscillator effect until the heat dries out the moisture or the contact bounce settles.

To address this without immediately replacing the entire assembly, you should inspect the ground straps connecting the relay to the chassis and the brake light circuit. Look for rust or paint on the grounding bolts; cleaning these points often resolves intermittent electrical gremlins. If the ground is solid, the relay itself may be internally compromised by corrosion that hasn't yet failed completely.

If you are working on a modern vehicle with similar issues, consider swapping the turn signal module to one with a sealed connector housing to prevent moisture ingress. For older vehicles like the Grand Cherokee, mechanical relays are susceptible to this exact type of environmental degradation. The solution is often less about replacing the part and more about ensuring the electrical environment around it is dry and grounded correctly.

For those looking for a modern equivalent or a reliable replacement, you might check out resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) to see if they carry sealed automotive relays that offer better protection against the very humidity issues causing this problem. The trade-off is cost versus reliability; a slightly more expensive, high-quality relay can prevent repeated diagnostics and eventual total failure of the signal system.
